A machine instruction typically includes opcode, operand specifiers, and optional immediate field. Opcode selects the operation, operands identify data sources/destinations, and immediate embeds a constant directly in instruction encoding.

entry.title: Which experimental metrics allow a sound comparison of two implementations (RISC and CISC)? Why is instruction count alone insufficient?

Use runtime, CPI, instructions retired, cache/TLB miss rates, branch mispredicts, energy, and throughput. Instruction count alone ignores instruction complexity, memory stalls, and microarchitectural effects, so it cannot predict true performance.

entry.title: How does using memoryview in Python reduce memory-copy overhead?

entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

memoryview exposes buffer-protocol data without creating a new copy. Slicing and passing views can reuse the same underlying bytes, reducing allocations and copy bandwidth costs in I/O and parsing pipelines.

entry.title: What value range can n-bit unsigned and signed integers represent? How is the overflow boundary determined?
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #47.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

Unsigned n-bit range is 0 to 2^n - 1. Signed two’s-complement n-bit range is -2^(n-1) to 2^(n-1)-1. Overflow boundary is crossed when arithmetic result lies outside these bounds.

entry.title: How does addressing mode affect the number of micro-operations during instruction execution? Give an example.
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #46.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

More complex addressing usually needs extra micro-operations for address generation and memory access. Example: ADD R1, [R2+R3*4+8] requires effective-address calculation and memory read before ALU add, while ADD R1, R4 is typically a simpler single ALU path.

entry.title: How is the number of offset bits computed for a page of size page_size? Give an example for 4 KiB.
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #45.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

Offset bits equal log2(page_size). For a 4 KiB page, page_size = 4096 = 2^12, so offset requires 12 bits.

entry.title: How does concurrent I/O by multiple processes affect performance? Which factors determine scalability?
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #44.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

Concurrent I/O can improve throughput by overlapping waits, but contention can also increase latency. Scalability depends on device queue depth, scheduler policy, lock contention, filesystem behavior, and bandwidth limits.

entry.title: What is a page fault? Which stages are included in operating-system handling?
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #43.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

A page fault occurs when a referenced virtual page is not currently mapped to resident physical memory. OS trap handler validates access, locates/loads page from disk if needed, updates page tables/TLB, then resumes the instruction.

entry.title: What is an addressing mode? Provide effective address (EA) formulas for register-indirect and base-index-displacement addressing.
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #42.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

Addressing mode defines how instruction operands are located. For register-indirect mode: EA = [Rbase]. For base-index-displacement mode: EA = Rbase + Rindex * scale + displacement (or EA = Base + Index + Disp in simpler ISAs).

entry.title: What is a system call, and what overhead accompanies it during I/O operations?
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #41.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

A system call is a controlled transition from user mode to kernel mode to request OS services. Overheads include mode switch, validation, copying, scheduling effects, and possible blocking. Batching I/O reduces syscall overhead per byte.

entry.title: What is a working set? How does the ratio between working set size and cache capacity affect program performance?
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #40.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

Working set is the active data footprint needed in a phase of execution. If it fits in cache, hit rate is high and performance is strong; if not, frequent evictions and misses slow the program significantly.

entry.title: What is a process working set? How does its size affect page fault frequency and system performance?
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #39.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

Working set is the set of pages actively used during a time window. If it exceeds available memory, page faults increase and performance drops due to thrashing. Keeping working set within memory limits is critical.

entry.title: What is cache memory? What is the role of a cache line in data exchange between the CPU and RAM?
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #38.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

Cache is a small fast memory storing recently/frequently used data from RAM. Data moves in cache lines (fixed-size blocks), which are the transfer unit between cache levels and memory. Locality determines how effectively each line is used.

entry.title: What is an Instruction Set Architecture (ISA), and how is it different from processor microarchitecture?
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #37.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

ISA is the programmer-visible contract: instructions, registers, addressing modes, and behavior. Microarchitecture is the internal implementation (pipelines, caches, execution units) that realizes the ISA. Different CPUs can share one ISA but differ in performance.

entry.title: What is the TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer), and what role does it play in speeding up memory access? Explain TLB hit vs TLB miss.
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #36.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

TLB is a small cache of recent virtual-to-physical page translations. TLB hit provides fast translation; TLB miss triggers page-table walk, adding latency. High TLB hit rate is essential for memory performance.

entry.title: Why can an instruction like ADD R1, [R2+4] be more expensive than LOAD + ADD in a RISC model, even with fewer instructions?
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #35.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

A memory-operand ADD combines address generation, memory read, and ALU work in one complex instruction. In RISC, separated LOAD + ADD often pipelines better, has simpler timing, and can overlap with other operations despite extra instruction count.

entry.title: Why can't 0.1 be represented exactly in binary floating-point? What are the consequences for computation?
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #34.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

0.1 has an infinite repeating representation in binary fractions, so float stores only an approximation. This introduces tiny rounding errors, affecting equality checks and long computations; tolerance-based comparisons are safer.

entry.title: Why is sequential file access usually more efficient than random access? What role does read-ahead play?
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #33.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

Sequential file access aligns with contiguous blocks and allows read-ahead to prefetch upcoming data. Random access defeats prefetching and causes more seeks/page misses. Therefore sequential reads usually achieve higher bandwidth.

entry.title: Why is floating-point addition not associative? How does this affect parallel summation results?
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #32.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

Floating-point addition rounds after each operation, so (a+b)+c may differ from a+(b+c). Parallel reductions change operation order, so final sums can vary slightly across thread counts and execution plans.

entry.title: Why does increasing chunk size usually improve throughput up to a certain limit?
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #31.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

Larger chunks amortize fixed overhead per request (syscalls, protocol headers, scheduling). Throughput rises until bottlenecks like cache pressure, queue delays, memory bandwidth, or device limits dominate.

entry.title: Why can large-stride memory access degrade performance? Explain this in terms of locality and limited TLB capacity.
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #30.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

Large stride weakens spatial locality and touches more pages per unit work. This increases cache misses and TLB misses because limited TLB entries cannot cover sparse page footprints efficiently. Performance degrades due to translation and memory stalls.

entry.title: Why is memory access more expensive than register access? Which hardware factors cause this?
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #29.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

Registers are on-core and accessed in very few cycles, while memory access traverses cache hierarchy and possibly DRAM. Latency, bandwidth limits, contention, and coherence traffic make memory accesses more expensive.

entry.title: Why can two O(N) algorithms show different execution times in practice?
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #28.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

Asymptotic complexity ignores constants and hardware effects. Different memory-access patterns, branch behavior, vectorization, and cache/TLB usage can make one O(N) algorithm much faster in practice than another.

entry.title: What is the idea of compensated summation (Kahan method)? What are its advantages and limitations?
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #27.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

Kahan summation keeps a compensation term for lost low-order bits during floating-point addition. It significantly reduces accumulated rounding error in long sums. It is slower than naive summation and still not exact for all cases.

entry.title: What is the fundamental RISC vs CISC trade-off in instruction count, instruction complexity, and average CPI?
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #26.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

RISC tends to use more simpler instructions with lower and more predictable CPI, while CISC may use fewer but more complex instructions with potentially higher CPI. Real performance depends on microarchitecture, compiler quality, and memory behavior, not instruction count alone.

entry.title: What is the difference between row-wise and column-wise traversal in row-major memory layout?
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #25.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

In row-major layout, row-wise traversal accesses contiguous memory and is cache-friendly. Column-wise traversal jumps by row length, causing poor locality and more misses. Therefore row-wise loops are usually much faster.

entry.title: What is the data-copying problem during transfer between system components? What does zero-copy mean?
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #24.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

Extra data copies consume CPU cycles, memory bandwidth, and cache capacity, increasing latency. Zero-copy techniques avoid redundant copies by sharing buffers or remapping pages between layers. This improves throughput and lowers overhead.

entry.title: What is the principle of paged memory organization? Why is page size chosen as a power of two?
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #23.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

Paging divides virtual and physical memory into fixed-size pages/frames and maps them via page tables. Power-of-two page sizes make offset extraction a simple bit operation and align naturally with binary hardware logic.

entry.title: What is the hardware interrupt mechanism, and how does it provide asynchronous I/O?
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #22.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

A device raises an interrupt to notify CPU that an event or I/O completion occurred. CPU saves context, executes an interrupt handler, and resumes interrupted work. This allows asynchronous I/O without busy waiting.

entry.title: What is the difference between hardware integer arithmetic and Python integer implementation?
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #21.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

Hardware integers are fixed-width and overflow modulo 2^n. Python integers are arbitrary precision objects that grow as needed, avoiding overflow but adding allocation and runtime overhead. This trades speed for correctness and convenience.

entry.title: State the principle of temporal locality. Under which conditions does data reuse improve performance?
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #20.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

Temporal locality means recently used data is likely used again soon. Performance improves when reuse happens before eviction from cache. Tight loops and small working sets typically benefit most.

entry.title: State the principle of spatial locality. Why is sequential array traversal cache-efficient?
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #19.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

Spatial locality means if one memory location is accessed, nearby locations are likely accessed soon. Sequential array traversal matches cache-line loading, so each fetched line serves multiple elements. This increases cache efficiency and lowers latency.

entry.title: State Amdahl's law. How does the serial code fraction affect maximum parallel speedup?
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #18.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

Amdahl’s law: Speedup(N) = 1 / (S + (1-S)/N), where S is serial fraction. As S grows, maximum speedup is capped by 1/S even with many cores. Therefore, reducing serial work is crucial for scalability.

entry.title: Explain how lab results confirm the impact of spatial and temporal locality on cache efficiency.
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #17.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

Experiments usually show faster execution for sequential and repeated access patterns than scattered one-pass patterns. Sequential access demonstrates spatial locality; repeated reuse demonstrates temporal locality. Higher hit rates directly correlate with lower runtime.

entry.title: Explain why increasing access stride reduces array-processing performance.
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #16.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

Larger stride skips nearby elements, reducing spatial locality and cache-line utilization. More cache and TLB misses occur, increasing memory stalls. As a result, throughput drops even with the same O(N) complexity.

entry.title: Explain the role of the I/O subsystem in a computing system and its place in the memory hierarchy.
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #15.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

The I/O subsystem connects CPU/memory with external devices and manages data movement via controllers, interrupts, and DMA. It sits outside core CPU caches but interacts through memory buffers and page cache. Its latency and bandwidth often bound end-to-end performance.

entry.title: Explain the Load/Store principle in RISC architecture. Why are arithmetic operations limited to register operands?
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #14.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

Load/store architecture separates memory access from arithmetic: LOAD/STORE move data, ALU ops use registers only. Register-only ALU operations simplify pipelines, timing, and decoding, enabling high-frequency and predictable execution.

entry.title: Explain the purpose of memory hierarchy in modern computing systems. What problem does it solve?
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #13.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

Memory hierarchy bridges the speed-capacity-cost gap between CPU registers and large storage. Small fast memories (registers/cache) hide latency of larger slower memories (DRAM/disk). It solves the memory wall by exploiting locality.

entry.title: Explain the purpose of virtual memory and its main benefits for process isolation and scalability.
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #12.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

Virtual memory gives each process a private address space independent of physical layout. It improves isolation, protection, and controlled sharing while allowing larger logical memory via paging. This supports multitasking and scalable workloads.

entry.title: Explain overflow in two's-complement arithmetic. Why is fixed-width arithmetic modular?
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #11.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

In two’s complement, overflow occurs when result exceeds representable range and wraps around. Fixed-width arithmetic operates modulo 2^n because higher bits are discarded. This is why integer operations behave as modular arithmetic at hardware level.

entry.title: Explain demand paging and the first-touch effect when initializing a large array.
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #10.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

Demand paging loads pages only when first accessed, not at allocation time. With first-touch, physical pages are committed when code first writes/reads them, so initialization pattern affects NUMA locality and startup latency. Sequential first-touch often yields better placement and cache behavior.

entry.title: Explain the trade-off between numeric precision and performance. When should you use decimal/Fraction and when standard float?
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #9.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

Higher-precision or exact numeric types improve correctness for financial/accounting or exact-rational workloads but are slower and memory-heavier. Standard float is much faster and suitable for scientific/engineering tasks tolerant to rounding noise. Choose based on error tolerance and domain requirements.

entry.title: Explain the difference between user-space buffering and the OS page cache.
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #8.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

User-space buffering is managed by application/runtime libraries to reduce syscall frequency. The OS page cache is kernel-managed and stores file pages to speed disk I/O across processes. They are different layers and may both affect performance.

entry.title: Describe the IEEE 754 double-precision format. What are the roles of the sign bit, exponent, and mantissa?
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #7.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

IEEE 754 double precision uses 64 bits: 1 sign bit, 11 exponent bits, and 52 fraction bits. The sign controls positive/negative, exponent sets scale, and fraction (mantissa/significand) stores precision bits. Together they represent a wide numeric range with finite precision.

entry.title: Describe the sequence of actions during virtual address translation by the MMU.
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #6.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

The MMU splits VA into VPN and offset, checks TLB for cached translation, and on TLB miss walks page tables in memory. If mapping exists, it gets the physical frame and forms physical address with offset. If mapping is invalid, a page fault is raised for OS handling.

entry.title: Provide the throughput formula and explain which factors can distort lab measurement results.
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #5.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

Throughput is amount of work per unit time, e.g., bytes/second or operations/second. Measurements can be distorted by warm-up effects, caching, background processes, thermal throttling, timer resolution, and small sample size. Repeated trials and controlled conditions improve reliability.

entry.title: Write the formula for CPI. How does CPI change if instruction count decreases but average instruction cost increases?
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #4.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

CPI is cycles per instruction: CPI = Total CPU Cycles / Instruction Count. If you reduce instruction count but make each instruction more expensive, CPI usually increases, while total runtime may increase or decrease depending on the net cycle count.

entry.title: Write the virtual address structure as VA=VPN∥Offset and explain each component.
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #3.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

Virtual address is split as VA = VPN || Offset, where VPN is the Virtual Page Number and Offset is the byte position inside the page. The MMU translates VPN to a physical frame number, and Offset is copied unchanged. This design enables page-based translation.

entry.title: Define cache hit and cache miss. How do they affect average memory access time?
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #2.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

A cache hit means the requested data is found in cache, while a cache miss means it must be fetched from a lower memory level. Average memory access time is roughly hit_time + miss_rate * miss_penalty. More hits reduce latency; more misses increase it.

entry.title: Define absolute and relative error. When is relative error preferable?
entry.summary: English Q&A note on systems and architecture topic #1.
entry.content:
Synthetic Notice: This is synthetic content created to test scrapers.

Absolute error is the difference between measured and true value: |x_measured - x_true|. Relative error is absolute error normalized by the true (or reference) value, usually in percent. Relative error is preferable when comparing accuracy across values with different scales.
